title: Risotto ai Funghi Porcini
subtitle: dried porcini and parmesan risotto
excerpt: Risotto ai funghi porcini uses dried porcini to build a deep, earthy stock and then adds the soaked mushrooms back into the rice as it cooks. The result is one of the most intensely flavoured of the Italian risotti. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Porcini risotto is a staple of northern Italian cooking, particularly in Lombardy, Piedmont, and Veneto, where the dried porcini trade through mountain markets supplied year-round access to an ingredient otherwise only available in autumn. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), includes several rice preparations with mushrooms that follow this basic logic: soaking dried mushrooms to create a flavoured liquid, then using that liquid as the risotto stock. The modern version adds the soaked mushrooms to the rice partway through cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Ceps (Boletus edulis) dried to concentrate their flavour. Soaking them in hot water produces a dark, earthy liquid that forms the base of the risotto stock. The soaked mushrooms are added to the rice.

The final step of risotto-making: stirring in cold butter and Parmesan off the heat until the rice is glossy and fluid. The name comes from manteca, a word for fat or lard in older Italian culinary language.

content.text: Risotto ai funghi porcini gets its flavour from two sources: the soaking liquid from

, which becomes the stock, and the mushrooms themselves, which go back into the pan as the rice cooks. Dried porcini smell strongly of earth and autumn forest; once soaked, that quality passes into the liquid. Used as stock, it turns a straightforward risotto into something considerably deeper.

at the end: taking the pan off the heat and stirring in cold butter with parmesan until the risotto is glossy and flows like thick porridge. This is what gives risotto its characteristic creaminess. Skip this step and the rice is good; do it properly and it is excellent.
Soak the porcini and prepare the stock

Put {{mushrooms-porcini-dried}} of dried porcini in a jug and cover with 300 ml of just-boiled water. Leave for 20 minutes. Lift the mushrooms out with a slotted spoon and chop them roughly. Strain the soaking liquid through a fine sieve to remove any grit and add it to {{stock-vegetable}} of hot vegetable stock in a saucepan. Keep warm over a low heat.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a wide, heavy-based pan over a medium heat. Add {{onion}} onion and cook gently for 8 minutes until soft and translucent. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and cook for 1 minute more.

Add {{arborio-rice}} of risotto rice and stir to coat in the oil. Cook for 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until the grains look slightly translucent at the edges. Add {{dry-white-wine}} of dry white wine and stir until absorbed.

Add the chopped porcini. Then begin adding the warm porcini-enriched stock a ladle at a time, stirring constantly and waiting for each addition to be absorbed before adding the next. This takes about 18 to 20 minutes. The rice should be cooked through but still have a slight bite at the centre.

Take the pan off the heat. Add {{unsalted-butter}} of cold cubed butter and {{parmesan}} of parmesan. Stir vigorously for 1 to 2 minutes until the butter melts and the risotto is glossy and flowing. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper. Add a splash of stock if it has tightened up.
Rest for 1 minute, then serve immediately in warm bowls. Add chopped parsley and extra parmesan at the table.

items.cause: Not enough stock added, or cooked past the point of done
items.fix: Risotto should flow when the plate is tilted. Add a splash of warm stock and stir vigorously before serving.

items.cause: Soaking liquid poured away, or porcini quality poor
items.fix: Always use the strained soaking liquid as part of the stock. Buy dried porcini from a supplier with turnover; old stock loses its potency.

items.symptom: Rice is chalky in the centre
items.fix: Continue adding stock and stirring. The grain is done when there is no white chalk at the centre; it should feel just firm when bitten, not hard.

items.cause: Heat too high, or not stirred often enough
items.fix: Keep the heat at medium throughout. Constant stirring is not strictly necessary but frequent stirring is: every 30 seconds or so.

content.text: Porcini risotto is northern Italian cooking at its most direct: rice from the Po valley, dried mushrooms from the Alps and Apennines, butter and Parmesan from Lombardy. In autumn, fresh porcini are available; in other seasons, dried porcini and their soaking liquid do the work. The soaking liquid is what gives the dish its depth. Use it all.
